    \begin{subequations} \label{subeq:H_appendix}
        \begin{align}
            DH(0) &= T, \qquad H(0) = 0, \\
            &F \circ H = H \circ A_1, \qquad \text{on $B_1^X$}. \label{eq:H_inv_appendix}
        \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    This map is unique among $C^{\ell+1}_b$ maps satisfying \eqref{subeq:H_appendix}.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
The only improvement Theorem~\ref{thm:appendix} brings to \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Cabre2003a} is that $\mathrm{im}(T)$ need not be closed and complemented.
    This is precisely the additional condition an immersion needs to satisfy in the Banach manifold setting \cite[Proposition~II.2.2]{lang2012fundamentals}.
    Hence $\mathrm{im}(H)$ obtained in Theorem~\ref{thm:appendix} can generally not be interpreted as an immersed submanifold of $Y$.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lemma:Cabre1}
    Assume \ref{A1}-\ref{A3}. 
    There exist a polynomial $H^\leq = \sum_{j=1}^\ell H_j$, where the $H_j$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $j$, such that $H_1 = T$ and
    \begin{equation}
        F \circ H^\leq(x) = H^\leq \circ A_1 (x) + O(\Vert x \Vert_X^{\ell+1})
        \label{eq:H_leq}
    \end{equation}
    as $x \to 0$.

    Moreover, if $H$ is any $C^\ell_b$ map satisfying \eqref{subeq:H_appendix}, then its $\ell$-jet must agree with $H^\leq$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
For simplicity, we assume $X$, $Y$ are complex; the real case follows as in \cite[Lemma 3.1]{Cabre2003a}. 
    We solve \eqref{eq:H_leq} order by order.
    At orders $0$ and $1$, the solution is provided by $H_1 = T$ and \ref{A2}.
    For $2 \leq j \leq \ell$, we solve equations of the form
    \begin{equation}
        A H_j - H_j[A_1 \cdot,\ldots,A_1 \cdot] = G_j,
        \label{eq:H_j}
    \end{equation}
    where $G_j$ is a known symmetric multilinear map $X \times \cdots \times X \to Y$ ($j$ copies of $X$) composed of lower order terms.
    The unique solvability of \eqref{eq:H_j} for $H_j$ follows from \cite[Proposition~3.2]{Cabre2003a}: Borrowing the notation from therein and setting 
    \begin{displaymath}
        \mathcal{L}_{j,A,B} : H_j \mapsto BH_j[A\cdot,\ldots,A\cdot]
    \end{displaymath}
    to act on the space of symmetric multilinear maps ${S}_j$, we have $\sigma(\mathcal{L}_{j,A,B}; {S}_j) \subset \sigma(B; Y) \sigma(A;X)^j$.
    Hence \eqref{eq:H_j}, which is equivalent to
    \begin{displaymath}
        \mathcal{L}_{j,\mathrm{id}_X,A} \left( \mathrm{id} - \mathcal{L}_{j,A_1,A^{-1}} \right) H_j = G_j,
    \end{displaymath}
    is uniquely solvable by the spectral assumptions \ref{A3} for all $2 \leq j \leq \ell$.
    
    The '$O$' form of the remainder follows by all maps being at least $C^{\ell+1}$. 

    If $H$ is a $C^\ell_b$ map satisfying \eqref{subeq:H_appendix}, its Taylor coefficients up to order $\ell$ must satisfy the same equations \eqref{eq:H_j}, to all of which the solutions are unique.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lemma:Cabre2}
    Let $s \geq \ell$ and assume \ref{A1}-\ref{A3}.
    Then $\mathcal{S}$ is an automorphism of $\Gamma_{s,\ell}$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
The proof of \cite[Lemma 3.3]{Cabre2003a} carries over to this setting, using the assumption \eqref{eq:norm_squeeze}.
    The proof is significantly simpler for our case herein (due to $A_1$ being linear); we spell the details out for completeness.

    We may write the operation $\mathcal{S}$ as the composition
    \begin{displaymath}
        \mathcal{L}_A \big( \mathrm{id}_{\Gamma_{s,\ell}} - \mathcal{L}_{A^{-1}} \mathcal{R}_{A_1}  \big),
    \end{displaymath}
    where $\mathcal{L}_B$ and $\mathcal{R}_B$ stand for left and right compositions (by $B$) acting on the space  $\Gamma_{s,\ell}$.
    It is clear that $\mathcal{L}_A$ is boundedly invertible on $\Gamma_{s,\ell}$; it remains to show $\Vert \mathcal{L}_{A^{-1}} \mathcal{R}_{A_1} \Vert_{L(\Gamma_{s,\ell})} < 1$.
    
    In fact, $\Vert \mathcal{L}_{A^{-1}} \Vert_{L(\Gamma_{s,\ell})} \leq \Vert A^{-1} \Vert_{L(Y)}$, hence it suffices to show $\Vert \mathcal{R}_{A_1} \Vert_{L(\Gamma_{s,\ell})} \leq \Vert A_1 \Vert_{L(X)}^{\ell+1}$ by \eqref{eq:norm_squeeze}.
    By virtue of $\Gamma_{s,\ell}$ and Taylor's formula, we have that
    \begin{displaymath}
        \Vert D^i H(x) \Vert \leq  \Vert H \Vert_{\Gamma_{s,\ell}} \Vert x \Vert_X^{\ell-i+1}, \qquad x \in B_1^X,
    \end{displaymath}
    for $0 \leq i \leq \ell$ and $H \in \Gamma_{s,\ell}$.
    Thus, considering $A_1 B_1^X \subset B_1^X$,
    \begin{align*}
        \Vert D^i( \mathcal{R}_{A_1}H ) (x) \Vert &= \Vert D^iH (A_1x)[A_1 \cdot,\ldots,A_1 \cdot] \Vert \\
        &\leq \Vert H \Vert_{\Gamma_{s,\ell}} \Vert A_1x \Vert_X^{\ell-i+1} \Vert A_1 \Vert_{L(X)}^{i}, \qquad x \in B_1^X, \; 1 \leq i \leq s.
    \end{align*}
    This shows $\Vert \mathcal{R}_{A_1} \Vert_{L(\Gamma_{s,\ell})} \leq \Vert A_1 \Vert_{L(X)}^{\ell+1}$ and hence the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lemma:Cabre3}
    Assume \ref{A1}-\ref{A3}.
    The operator $\mathcal{T}:\Gamma_{s,\ell} \to \Gamma_{s,\ell}$ admits a unique fixed point, $\ell \leq s \leq r-1$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
The proof carries over unchanged from \cite[Lemma~3.4]{Cabre2003a}, except one no longer has to restrict to the ball of radius one in $\Gamma_{s,\ell}$ on account of our global assumption of $\Vert F -A \Vert_{C_b^r(Y)}$ being sufficiently small in \ref{A1}.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lemma:AD1}
    Assume \ref{appD_ass1}-\ref{appD_ass2}.
    There exists $\rho >0$ such that for every $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, the map $h_\theta: N_\theta(\rho) \to h_\theta(N_\theta(\rho) )$ is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Pointwise in $\theta$, this is simply an application of the inverse function theorem \cite[Theorem~4.5]{lee2003smooth} using the assumptions in \ref{appD_ass1}.
    That $\rho>0$ can be chosen uniformly with respect to $\theta$ follows from the uniform continuity assumptions of \ref{appD_ass2}, which in particular permit a choice of $\rho$ for which $\sup_{\theta \in \mathbb{R}, |x| < \rho}\Vert \imath_{N_\theta \xhookrightarrow{} \mathbb{R}^n}-Dh_\theta(x) \Vert < 1/2$.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lemma:AD2}
    Assume \ref{appD_ass1}-\ref{appD_ass2}. 
    Let $\rho$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lemma:AD1}, and denote by $\xi: \zeta( \mathscr{N}(\rho)) \to  \mathscr{N}(\rho)$ the map $(\theta,y) \mapsto (\theta,h_\theta^{-1}(y))$.
    Then $(\theta,y) \mapsto D_2^j\xi(\theta,y)$ is continuous for $0 \leq j \leq k$ and uniformly continuous at $\mathbb{R} \times \{0\}$ for $j = 0,1$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
It suffices to show the stated continuity properties for the map $\eta:= \mathrm{proj}_2 \circ \xi =(\theta,y) \mapsto h_\theta^{-1}(y)$.
    Define
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal{T} : \mathscr{N}(\rho) \ni (\theta,x) \mapsto x-h(\theta,x) \in \mathbb{R}^n,
    \end{align*}
    and note that $\eta(\theta,y) = \mathcal{T}(\theta,\eta(\theta,y))+y$ for all $(\theta,y) \in \zeta( \mathscr{N}(\rho))$; and that $\mathcal{T}$ is a uniform contraction on the second factor by the choice of $\rho$ (see the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:AD1}).
    Let $\mathrm{Lip}_2(\mathcal{T}) <1$ denote this contraction constant.
    Then, for $(\theta,y)$ and $(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})$ in $\zeta( \mathscr{N}(\rho))$, 
    \begin{align*}
        |\eta(\theta,y) - \eta(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})| &\leq |y-\tilde{y}|  + |\mathcal{T}(\theta,\eta(\theta,y)) - \mathcal{T}(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})) | \\
        & \leq |y-\tilde{y}|  + |\mathcal{T}(\theta,\eta(\theta,y)) - \mathcal{T}(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\theta,y)) |  \\
        & + | \mathcal{T}(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\theta,y)) - \mathcal{T}(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})) | \\
        &\leq |y-\tilde{y}|  + |h(\theta,\eta(\theta,y)) - h(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\theta,y)) | \\
        &+ \mathrm{Lip}_2(\mathcal{T}) |\eta(\theta,y) - \eta(\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})| \\
        &\leq (1-\mathrm{Lip}_2(\mathcal{T}))^{-1}[|y-\tilde{y}|  + |h(\theta,\eta(\theta,y)) - h(\tilde{\theta},\eta(\theta,y)) |]
    \end{align*}
    The continuity and uniform continuity properties thus follow from those of $h$ (noting that $|(\theta,y) - (\tilde{\theta},\tilde{y})|$ can be controlled by the canonical distance on $\zeta( \mathscr{N}(\rho))$).

    For the higher order derivatives, we simply employ the chain rule:
    \begin{displaymath}
         D_2 \eta(\theta,y) = [Dh_\theta(\eta(\theta,y))]^{-1}.
    \end{displaymath}
    Since inversion is a $C^\infty$ operation, it follows by the continuity properties of $(\theta,x) \mapsto D^jh_\theta(x)$ assumed in \ref{appD_ass2} and induction that $\eta$ satisfies the same properties.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
